courses.title: Data Play: Sort, Count and Teach a Computer

Sort, count and show data with picture graphs

modules.title: Module 1 · Notice and Wonder

items.title: 2.1 Are Sprinters Getting Faster?

items.problem: Students want to predict the 2028 winning time; eyeballing isn't enough, so they need a rate of change and an equation.
items.need: Students want to predict the 2028 winning time; eyeballing isn't enough, so they need a rate of change and an equation.

Plot year vs time in CODAP; add a movable line, then a least-squares line.

Interpret slope as seconds per year and test predictions

items.check: Write the model, interpret the slope in a sentence with units, and name one reason the prediction for 2400 is unreasonable.

trend_line.idea: Draw one straight line through the middle of the dots. It gives you a simple rule: when this goes up, that goes up or down by about this much.
terms: how much y changes for each step in x
reading the line at a new x

residuals.idea: Each dot sits a little above or below the line. Those little gaps are called residuals. If the gaps are small and mixed up, your line is doing a good job.
terms: a curve in the residuals means try another model
adding up squared residuals measures fit

correlation.idea: Two things can go up together without one causing the other. Ice cream sales and sunburns both rise in summer. The sun is the real reason!
terms: one change makes the other happen

lines_cross.idea: When two lines cross, both rules give the same answer at that spot. Before it one choice is better, and after it the other one wins.
terms: the x and y that fit both
left of the point one option wins, right of it the other

lin_vs_exp.idea: Linear growth adds the same amount every time. Exponential growth doubles or multiplies, so it starts slowly and then shoots up fast.

decay.idea: Some things shrink by a share each time, like hot cocoa cooling down. They drop fast at first and then slow down.

log_scale.idea: On a log scale, each step up means ten times bigger. It helps you fit tiny and giant numbers on the same graph.

logistic.idea: Lots of things grow fast and then level off, making an S-shaped curve. Computers use the same curve to turn a score into a chance, like 80% sure.

parabola.idea: When you throw a ball, it rises, stops at the top and falls. That curve is called a parabola, and its top point shows the highest the ball went.

cost_bowl.idea: A computer learns by checking how wrong it is, then taking a small step to be a bit less wrong. It's like walking downhill until you reach the bottom.
terms: a number for how wrong the model is
the slope at the current point

overfitting.idea: If a model twists and turns to touch every single dot, it is just memorising. It then guesses badly on new data. Simple often works better.
terms: great on training data, poor on new data
data kept back to test the model
more bends is not always better

train_test.idea: We teach the computer with most of the data and hide the rest. Then we test it on the hidden part to see if it really learned.
terms: examples kept hidden until the end
share of test answers it gets right

neural_net.idea: A neural network passes numbers through layers, a bit like a relay race. Each link has a strength that gets tuned as the network practises.
terms: how strongly one neuron affects the next

decision_tree.idea: A decision tree plays twenty questions with the data. It asks yes or no questions, one after another, until it reaches an answer.
terms: a question that divides the data
how many questions in a row

clusters.idea: Clustering puts similar things into groups without being told the answers. It's like sorting a messy toy box into neat piles.
terms: how many groups we ask for

classify_examples.idea: Instead of writing rules, we show the computer lots of labelled examples. It spots the pattern and can then label new things by itself.
terms: the right answer for an example

rules_vs_examples.idea: A normal program follows rules that people write. Machine learning works out its own rules by looking at examples.

data_cycle.idea: Every data project goes round a loop: ask, collect, show, explain. The answer usually leads to an even better question.
terms: say what it means and what it cannot show

dataset_table.idea: A dataset is just a table. Each row is one thing you measured, each column is one fact about it, and units tell you what the numbers mean.
terms: one row, one thing we measured

misleading_graph.idea: The same numbers can look huge or tiny depending on how the graph is drawn. Bars should start at zero, and everything should have a label.

pictograph.idea: Sort things into groups, count each group, and draw a picture for each one. The longest row shows the most.

shapes.idea: Look for shapes around you, count them and build towers with blocks. The tallest tower shows the shape you found most.

weather.idea: If you check the weather every day, you are collecting data! A chart helps you see which days were the sunniest.

robot_grid.idea: An algorithm is a list of exact steps. Robots follow them in order, so every step has to be really clear.

pattern.idea: A pattern repeats in a way you can predict. Once you spot the rule, you can say what comes next.

flowchart.idea: Programs make choices (if this, do that) and repeat things (loops). A flowchart draws the path one step at a time.
terms: a stored value, like the score

design_cycle.idea: Engineers design, build, test and improve. Every test gives them data to make the next version better.
terms: change one thing at a time

fairness.idea: A model can work well for one group of people and badly for another. Checking each group helps you see if it is fair.
terms: a check before using the model

matrix.idea: A spreadsheet is a grid of numbers: rows are examples and columns are features. A model mixes the features to make its guess.

one_hot.idea: Computers need numbers, so a word like red, green or blue becomes a row of 0s with a single 1. Each colour gets its own column.

confusion.idea: A confusion matrix is a scoreboard of right and wrong answers. It shows exactly which mistakes the model makes.
terms: all correct answers over all answers
says yes when it is no

sensor.idea: A sensor takes a measurement every second. A line graph shows how things changed and the moment something happened.

anomaly.idea: An anomaly shows how different something is from normal. Bars above zero were warmer than usual, and bars below were cooler.

bubbles.idea: Each bubble is a country: money across, health up, and size for how many people live there. Richer countries tend to live longer, but not always.
terms: a point far from the pattern

word_freq.idea: Words can be data too! Count which words appear most, and even the little everyday words can work like a writer's fingerprint.
terms: a number that describes the text

sentiment.idea: Sentiment analysis gives words a happy or sad score. Graph it chapter by chapter and you can see the shape of a story.

heart_rate.idea: After running, your heart rate drops fast and then settles. The faster it drops, the fitter your heart is.

survey.idea: A survey turns what people do into data. A scatter plot shows if two habits go together, but not why.
terms: a link we can see in the data

supply_demand.idea: Where what sellers offer meets what buyers want, they agree on a price. That meeting point is where the lines cross.
terms: how much sellers offer at each price

forecast.idea: A forecast stretches a trend into the future. The range gets wider the further ahead you look, because the future is uncertain.

playground.idea: Measure different surfaces at the same time so the test is fair. Then you can find the safest places to play.
terms: use data to suggest a change

travel.idea: A class survey can become a bar chart. One look at the longest bar answers the question.
terms: a group like walk or bus

notebook.idea: A notebook mixes code, results and notes in one place. Run one cell at a time and see what happens straight away.
terms: a block of code or text
Shift and Enter runs a cell

histogram.idea: A histogram groups numbers into ranges to show how they spread out. Look for the middle, the spread and anything unusual.
terms: a value far from the rest

sound_pose.idea: Sounds become wave numbers and poses become points on your body. Anything that can become numbers can teach a model.
terms: body positions as x and y

house_price.idea: A model looks at past house sales to learn how price changes with size. Then it can guess the price of a house it has never seen.
terms: how far off the guess is

ai_helpers.idea: AI already helps us every day. For each helper, ask: who does it help, and what could go wrong?

responsible_ai.idea: Good AI asks three questions. Is it fair? Did people agree to share their data? Can we trust what it makes?

notice_wonder.idea: Great data work starts with noticing things and wondering about them. A wonder can turn into a question you answer with data.

guess_check.idea: Make a guess first, then count to check. Seeing how close you were helps you make an even better guess next time.

checklist.idea: Before you trust some data, ask where it came from, how it was collected, what might be missing and whether you may use it.

records_cross.idea: Two trend lines might cross one day far in the future, but times can't keep falling forever. Guesses far beyond your data are risky.

labs.title: Colab Lab: Your First Model in Python
steps: Load 30 Olympic winning times into pandas and graph them.
Adjust slope and intercept by hand to lower the error.
Let LinearRegression find the best line and compare.
Train on Games up to 2000 and test on 2004-2024.
Predict 2028 and find the year the line reaches 0 seconds.

labs.title: Colab Lab: Linear or Exponential?
steps: Load the UN billion milestones and graph them.
Compute the percent growth rate between milestones.
Fit a linear model and an exponential model to 1960-2022.
Compare their errors.
Predict 2050 and compare with the UN projection of about 9.7 billion.
